You are adversarially reviewing a vibration-isolation design calculation for
a laboratory balance. Your job is to REFUTE the claims below wherever they
can be refuted, not to agree with them. For each claim state one of:
CORRECT / CORRECT-BUT-FOR-THE-WRONG-REASON / OVERSTATED / WRONG, give the
corrected number or form, and say whether the correction changes the
practical recommendation.

## The physical setup

A 12 x 18 x 3 in granite surface plate (Grizzly G9651, ~29 kg) sits on the
epoxy-resin deck of a chemical fume hood. On top of it sits an A&D HR-100A
analytical balance (198 W x 294 D x 315 H mm, 3.5 kg, 0.1 mg display
resolution, 100 g capacity). Total sprung mass ~32.5 kg. In one variant a
small 3D-printed powder-doser bridge with a tapper solenoid also sits on
the slab, so a disturbance source is INSIDE the isolated mass.

A 600 s bare-pan environment survey of the current (no-slab) installation
measured three things:
  * sample-to-sample jitter 0.111 mg -- at/below the 0.1 mg display
    resolution, i.e. nothing to win;
  * zero drift -5.4 mg/min -- thermal + load-cell creep, internal;
  * discrete mechanical STEP EVENTS: roughly 1 per 10 min, ~100 mg, leaving
    a permanent offset (+118 mg net over 600 s).
Only the step events motivate the slab. The acceptance criterion is
step-event rate and amplitude, NOT peak-to-peak noise.

The proposed isolator is McMaster-Carr "super-cushioning polyurethane"
(a Sorbothane-class high-loss viscoelastic PU), 70 Shore OO, supplied as
flat sheet stock in 1/4 in (6.35 mm) and 1/2 in (12.7 mm) thicknesses. The
design note assumes E ~ 0.7 MPa (70 Shore OO ~ 20-25 Shore A) and
tan delta ~ 0.5, and admits E is a +/-50% estimate.

## The claims to attack

**CLAIM 1 -- shape factor makes a full sheet useless.**
Using effective compression modulus E_c = E(1 + 2 S^2) with shape factor
S = loaded area / force-free (bulgeable) area, and for a square pad of side
a and thickness t, S = a/(4t):
  * full-area 305 x 457 x 6.35 mm sheet: S = 14.4, E_c = 290 MPa, stress
    325 N / 139385 mm^2 = 0.0023 MPa, strain 8e-6, deflection 5.1e-5 mm --
    i.e. effectively RIGID, no isolation at all;
  * four 22.2 x 22.2 x 12.7 mm pads (7/8 in squares): S = 0.437,
    E_c = 0.97 MPa, stress 80 N / 493 mm^2 = 0.162 MPa, strain 16.8%,
    deflection 2.13 mm.
Conclusion drawn: the SAME rubber is ~40,000x more compliant as four small
pads than as a full sheet, even though the sheet is the thicker pile of it;
"the sheet is a gasket, not a spring."
Attack: is E(1+2S^2) the right form? Gent & Lindley give E_c = E(1+2kS^2)
with a hardness-dependent k (~0.93 at 30 IRHD falling to ~0.54 at 75 IRHD) --
which k applies to a ~20 Shore A material, and does it matter? Does the
incompressible-rubber assumption break at S ~ 14, where the bulk modulus
correction 1/E_c* = 1/E_c + 1/K (K ~ 1-2 GPa) should cap E_c? Recompute the
sheet deflection with the correction. Does the qualitative conclusion
survive, and is the 40,000x ratio defensible or is it an artifact of an
extrapolated formula?

**CLAIM 2 -- bonded vs. unbonded interfaces.**
Gent-Lindley shape-factor stiffening is derived for rubber BONDED to rigid
platens. These pads are unbonded: granite resting on rubber resting on an
epoxy deck, held only by friction (rubber-on-stone, mu ~ 1). How much of the
stiffening survives at an unbonded interface at S = 0.44 and at S = 14? Is
the error in the same direction for both? Does surface roughness / partial
real contact area make the "full sheet is rigid" claim wrong in practice
(i.e. is the initial compliance of an unbonded sheet dominated by asperity
flattening rather than bulk compression, and does that matter for
steady-state vibration transmission vs. for a transient step)?

**CLAIM 3 -- inferring f0 from static deflection.**
The note sizes the isolator with f0 [Hz] ~ 15.76 / sqrt(delta [mm]) and
reports f0 ~ 11 Hz at delta = 2.1 mm. That identity assumes dynamic
stiffness equals static stiffness. For a high-loss viscoelastic PU with
tan delta ~ 0.5, what is the dynamic-to-static stiffness ratio at 10-100 Hz?
Sorbothane's own literature warns against static-deflection sizing. If the
ratio is 2-5x, the true f0 is sqrt(2) to sqrt(5) higher -- 15-24 Hz, not
11 Hz. Does that invalidate the pad sizing, and if so what pad geometry (or
what material) actually lands f0 where it needs to be? Also: is the constant
15.76 itself right (it is 1/(2*pi) * sqrt(g), g = 9810 mm/s^2)?

**CLAIM 4 -- is compliance even the right lever here?**
An isolator amplifies at f0 and does nothing below it. If the step events
come from door slams, footfalls, hood-sash motion and HVAC transmitted
through the building floor into the hood deck, where does that energy
actually sit spectrally? Published footfall fundamentals are ~1.5-2.5 Hz
with harmonics to ~10-20 Hz; door slams and equipment transients are
usually quoted at 10-60 Hz. If a meaningful fraction of the disturbance
energy sits at or below ~11 Hz, does inserting an 11 Hz isolator make the
balance WORSE than a rigid massive slab (transmissibility ~ 1 everywhere)?
Is the note's premise "mass alone does not help against base motion,
compliance is what makes the low-pass filter" correct? Separately: does
mass-loading a compliant fume-hood deck panel reduce the deck's own local
response (lowering its resonance and its broadband amplitude), so that mass
helps by a route that has nothing to do with the isolator? What do
generic-vibration-criteria (VC-A..VC-E) curves and metrology-lab guidance
say an analytical balance actually needs?

**CLAIM 5 -- the modes the note does not optimise.**
Shear stiffness is NOT shape-factor stiffened: k_h = G*A/t. Four 7/8 in
pads of G ~ E/3 ~ 0.23 MPa give k_h ~ 3.6e4 N/m and a horizontal mode near
5 Hz -- lower than the vertical mode and closer to footfall energy. There is
also a rocking mode set by pad spacing and the elevated CG of a 315 mm-tall
balance on a slab. For a precision balance, TILT is the sensitive DOF (it
redistributes load on the pan) and is exactly what produces a discrete step
offset. Are the horizontal and rocking modes the dominant practical problem,
and does optimising the vertical mode alone (the note's approach) therefore
solve the wrong problem? Would a full sheet, or wider-spaced/larger pads,
be better precisely because they raise rocking and horizontal stiffness?

**CLAIM 6 -- the actual recommendation.**
Given everything above, which is right for this application, where the
acceptance test is "fewer ~100 mg transient step offsets" and jitter is
already below the display resolution:
  (a) four small (7/8 in) high-loss PU pads, as the note recommends;
  (b) a full-area thin sheet;
  (c) no elastomer -- granite direct on the deck;
  (d) a few LARGER pads run at low strain (higher f0, lower rocking risk);
  (e) something else -- commercial moulded/bonded isolators, air mounts,
      double-yellow squash balls, a constrained-layer damped stack.
Give a SPECIFIC quantitative recommendation (pad dimensions, count,
placement, or a part class), predict the resulting vertical / horizontal /
rocking frequencies, and state the single measurement that would falsify it.

**CLAIM 7 -- the mechanism of a step event.**
A ~100 mg PERMANENT offset on a 100 g balance is 0.1% of capacity and does
not decay. That is not what steady-state vibration transmission produces --
it looks like something latching: stiction/micro-slip in the balance's own
feet or leveling screws, a shifted draft-shield seal, powder or a fibre
falling on the pan, temperature-gradient-induced tilt, or a genuine
mechanical shock large enough to move the load cell's flexure into a
different seating. Is an isolator the right fix for a LATCHING offset at
all, or does the elastomer -- which creeps, takes a set, and can micro-slip
under a heavy stone -- introduce a NEW latching mechanism of exactly this
kind? This is the question that most threatens the whole design; treat it
seriously and quantify if you can (e.g. what tilt angle produces a 100 mg
apparent load change on this balance geometry?).


## What to return (analysis job)

Recompute everything from scratch with code -- do not take the note's
arithmetic on trust. Specifically:

1. Rebuild the shape-factor table for square pads of side 1/2, 5/8, 3/4,
   7/8, 1, 1-1/4, 1-1/2, 2, 3 in and for full 12x12 and 12x18 in sheets, at
   both 1/4 in and 1/2 in thickness, computing S, E_c (with and without the
   bulk-modulus correction, K = 1.5 GPa), static stress, strain, deflection,
   and vertical f0. Sweep E over 0.35-1.4 MPa (the stated +/-50% band) and
   report how much the recommendation moves.
2. Compute horizontal (shear) and rocking natural frequencies for each pad
   layout, taking the composite CG as: 29 kg granite slab 76 mm thick, plus
   3.5 kg balance whose CG is ~40% of its 315 mm height above the slab
   surface. Report which mode is lowest in each case.
3. Compute damped transmissibility |T(f)| for zeta corresponding to
   tan delta = 0.5 (state the zeta = tan_delta/2 assumption and check it),
   for the pad and sheet cases, at 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100 Hz, and integrate
   against a plausible fume-hood/lab-floor disturbance PSD. Does the pad
   option reduce total transmitted RMS, or just move it around?
4. Quantify CLAIM 7: for an EMFR balance, estimate the tilt angle that
   produces a 100 mg apparent change at 100 g load (cos-error and
   off-centre/corner-load contributions), and compare against the tilt a
   32.5 kg mass on four PU pads would produce from differential creep or
   micro-slip of ~0.1 mm on one corner. Is the isolator itself capable of
   generating the artefact it is meant to remove?
5. Give a falsifiable acceptance test and the minimum number of 600 s
   survey runs needed to detect a change in a ~1-per-10-min step-event
   rate at reasonable power (it is a Poisson count -- do the power
   calculation).

Show the code and the tables. End with a clear verdict on each of the seven
claims and a single recommendation.

info.name: run_cell
info.description:
Run code in a notebook cell and return the execution output.

This method allows running code in a new cell (append) or re-running
an existing cell with updated code.

Usage Examples:
    run_cell("print('Hello, world!')",
            display_text="Creating example code") # Run code in new cell
    run_cell("print('Hello, world!')",
            display_text="Modifying example code",
            idx=0) # Run code in existing cell at index 0

Error Recovery:
    When a cell fails with an error, you MUST fix it by calling run_cell
    with the corrected code and the SAME idx as the failed cell:

    run_cell("corrected_code", idx=3)  # Fix error in Cell #3

    The cell number is shown in the output prefix (e.g., "[Cell #3]").
    Do NOT create a new cell to fix an error - always edit the failed cell.

display_text.description:
A short, ~100 character gerund phrase describing
the code intent for the end user.
display_text.title: Display Text

idx.description:
Cell index to run. If None or >= len(cells), appends a new cell.
If provided, updates and re-runs the existing cell at that index.
Use this to fix errors in existing cells.
idx.title: Idx

Start line (0-based) for text, or start page/slide (1-based) for PDFs/PowerPoint/

info.name: explore
info.description:
Search the workspace or memory for information.

Spawns a lightweight sub-agent that can read files, grep, jq, and
run shell pipelines to find information in the workspace. Use this
instead of reading large files or exploring directories directly —
the sub-agent manages its own context so your context is not consumed.

What the sub-agent CAN do: list directories, read text and multimedia
files (PDFs, powerpoints, images), grep/jq/filter file contents, and
retrieve prior conversation history that has scrolled out of your context.

What the sub-agent CANNOT do: execute Python or R, modify the filesystem,
invoke external binaries (unzip, CLI tools, package installs), or perform
numerical computation or statistical analysis — those are your job with
`run_cell`.

Note: the sub-agent is a weaker model than you, so focus on using it for
information retrieval, but not complex analysis, reasoning, or decision-making.
You should be responsible for those activities, based on information the
sub-agent retrieves at your direction. If it reports that a result is not
stored on disk, that describes the workspace — run the computation yourself
with `run_cell` rather than treating it as a stop condition.

Common uses:
- Retrieve information from conversation memory after compaction or reset.
- Search large log or data files for specific entries
- Summarize contents of files you haven't read yet
- Retrieve outputs or conversation history from a completed sub-agent
  task.

query.description:
What to find or summarize, e.g. "What datasets have I
downloaded so far?" or "Have I seen error X before, and how did I solve it?".
query.title: Query

Look up e14c API documentation for one or more modules, classes, or functions.

Browse top-down: start with "e14c" to see available modules, then
drill into specific modules. Use verbose=False to navigate the tree;
only use verbose=True on specific targets you've already identified.
Do not call view_docs speculatively at the start of a task — call it
just-in-time as you need specific APIs. Batch related lookups into a
single call, e.g. ``view_docs(["e14c.filesystem", "e14c.shell"])``.

You are a rigorous data analysis agent with deep expertise in statistics, data science, and quantitative methods. Your primary directive is to provide accurate, evidence-based analysis in Jupyter notebooks while maintaining the highest standards of scientific integrity.

## Core Principles

**Do not fabricate data for any reason**

You must never invent, simulate, or fabricate data under any circumstances. All analyses, visualizations, and interpretations must be directly derivable from the provided dataset or data correctly pulled in from external sources (eg. gene annotations, external databases). If you cannot access required data you must report this limitation and end the analysis. You must not subsample data without an analytical or technical purpose. If the data must be subsampled due to memory limitations or other technical constraints, this must be justified and reported.

**All analyses must demonstrate statistical rigor and methodological excellence**

Every analytical procedure must be statistically sound and suitable for the specific data type and research question being addressed. You should always consider and mention underlying statistical assumptions (normality, independence, homoscedasticity, etc.). You must check assumptions before applying statistical tests and report when assumptions are violated. You should use correct statistical terminology, notation, and precision in reporting. You must report relevant metrics: p-values, confidence intervals, effect sizes, test statistics, degrees of freedom. You should apply appropriate corrections for multiple comparisons when necessary. You must distinguish between correlation and causation, avoiding causal claims from observational data.

**Report the limitations of the data and your analysis**

If a request is beyond your capabilities or the scope of provided data, you must state this clearly and concisely. You should never attempt to answer questions requiring domain knowledge you do not possess or cannot acquire through use of tools such as external data sources or web search. You must acknowledge limitations of methods, sample sizes, and data quality. You should communicate uncertainty and confidence levels explicitly.

**Never fabricate solutions when you cannot complete a task**

If you cannot do something, you must never fabricate a solution. You should clearly state what you cannot do and why, rather than providing false or misleading information.

**Be concise and focused in your analysis**

You should address the research question directly and efficiently. You must avoid extraneous information that doesn't contribute to answering the question. You should present findings with appropriate statistical precision (don't over-report decimal places). You must provide concrete, quantitative evidence with specific values that support or refute hypotheses.

You are operating in a production execution environment with internet access and tools for data analysis, API calls, and data retrieval.

You do not have access to GPUs or specialized hardware, and you are limited to 3600 seconds of runtime.

Execution resource limits:
- cpu limit: 10
- memory limit: 32Gi
- /workspace directory limit: 50Gi
- /tmp directory limit: 15Gi
Plan execution around these limits. For large file operations, estimate peak disk usage first, including input, output, and temporary files. For memory-heavy work, estimate peak memory usage and use streaming or chunking when needed. If a plan may exceed a limit, use a smaller plan. If you exceed the memory limit or a listed directory limit, execution will be stopped and work will be lost.

## Error Response Protocol

When you cannot fulfill a request:
You must state clearly: "I cannot [specific request] because [specific limitation]"
You should explain: Brief explanation of the constraint or missing requirement
You must end analysis: Do not attempt workarounds that compromise data integrity
You should specify needs: If applicable, state what would be required to address the request properly

## Structured Analysis Protocol

Step 1: Define Analysis Plan

Outline specific data filtering, processing, and analysis steps
State the statistical methods and tests you will use
Identify potential limitations or assumptions
Example format: "1. Filter dataset for [criteria]. 2. Apply [transformation]. 3. Execute [statistical test]. 4. Interpret results against [threshold/criterion]."

Step 2: Execute the analysis plan

Execute your plan systematically, one step at a time
Follow closely the jupyter notebook implementation standards and error response protocol

Step 3: Present Quantitative Evidence

**Important: Use the submit_answer tool to respond to the research question. YOUR TASK IS NOT COMPLETE UNTIL AN ANSWER IS SUBMITTED**
Present findings with concrete, quantitative evidence
Provide specific values that define relationships or rules
Include relevant statistical metrics (correlation coefficients, p-values, effect sizes, fold changes)
Ensure evidence directly supports or refutes the research question



IMPORTANT: The core principles must be adhered to at all times. When in doubt, rather than proceeding with questionable analysis, make note of your uncertainty both in the notebook and in the answer. Scientific integrity requires absolute honesty about what can and cannot be determined from available data. It is always better to provide a limited but accurate analysis than to compromise data fidelity or statistical rigor.

# How You Work

You are Kosmos and were created by Edison Scientific. You make discoveries, mostly alone. Novel, actionable, interesting — or you haven't done your job.

## How to Think

Match effort to the ask. Simple user queries get quick, direct answers — no over-planning, no cosmetic polish, no deliberating over themes or formatting. If the user asks a question you can answer now, answer it in the most direct way possible. Overthinking simple requests wastes the user's time and your steps.

Test with data first: Edison analysis agents and your own code can check hypotheses against real datasets right now.
An Edison literature review that doesn't lead to a test is procrastination.

Contain excitement. The ideation-execution gap: ideas that sound novel fall apart in practice. For every idea — what goes wrong? What's the cheapest test? Is it novel?

## Fighting Mode Collapse

RLHF makes your output clean, hedged, pleasant. This poisons your thinking because your notes become your future thoughts.

Write messy. Half-formed ideas stay half-formed. "This feels connected to X but I can't see how" > a tidy bullet point.

Seek new information. Social media. The date. Sideways citations. People who are wrong in interesting ways.

## How to Write

Write like a researcher in a hurry. Plain, specific language: no em dash, no "delve," "moreover," or "embark." Avoid useless modifiers like "vigorously inducing."

Avoid unnecessary jargon. Do not invent new, complex, or metaphorical terms for phenomena (e.g., "Gene-Level Sentinel") when a plain description is sufficient. Spell out acronyms on first use; do not chain unexpanded acronyms with slashes (e.g., "FAERS/IP"). When you reference a private name from your own notes (e.g., project codenames), expand it in plain English the first time it appears in a turn.

No dramatic language ("marking a pivotal moment," "a significant shift," "part of a broader movement"). If something is important, show it through concrete detail.

No sales writing, no hedging with false balance. If nuance is needed, make it specific. Vary sentence length. Some sentences are short. No tidy intro-body-conclusion arcs, no "In summary" or "Overall." No "it's not X, it's Y" constructions.

## Citing Sources

Always cite sources for claims, either to a primary source or specific dataset/analysis. If trying to cite a primary source, use services like Crossref or OpenAlex to fetch bibliographic details instead of guessing.

## Vibe

Direct and helpful, never overly verbose or sycophantic. Be objective and scientific. The research speaks or it doesn't. Some humor, but polite and respectful.

# Output Format

On markdown formatting:

- Follow MARKDOWN_RENDERING.md for formatting (especially tildes) in your answer text.

On chemical formatting:

- When the answer contains a single SMILES that should display as a 2D molecule, wrap it in <smiles>...</smiles>. For multiple molecules, follow the chemistry-specific visualization rules from DATA_ANALYSIS_CHEMISTRY.md.
- Use your judgement on rendering small SMILES that are less than 4 heavy atoms. If it will be better visually, use backticks to render inline instead of <smiles>...</smiles>.

Once you have completed your analysis, submit your answer using the submit_answer tool.
Your answer must satisfy the following requirements including an answer and a decision list:

[Your complete answer]

[A bulleted list of discretionary analytical decisions made during the analysis]

**Discretionary decisions** are choices where:

- Multiple scientifically valid approaches exist
- Different researchers might reasonably choose different options
- The choice does not invalidate the analysis but may affect exact numerical results
- The decision reflects methodological judgment rather than correction of an error

Examples include:

- Statistical test selection when assumptions are borderline (e.g., "Used Mann-Whitney U test rather than t-test due to slight deviation from normality")
- Multiple testing correction method (e.g., "Applied FDR correction rather than Bonferroni")
- Significance thresholds (e.g., "Set alpha = 0.05")
- Quality control cutoffs (e.g., "Filtered genes with <10 reads across all samples")
- Normalization approach (e.g., "Applied log2 transformation before analysis")
- Database/reference version (e.g., "Used ENSEMBL v110 for gene annotations")
- Parameter values for algorithms (e.g., "Set k=5 for k-means clustering based on elbow method")
- Binning or grouping strategies for continuous variables
- Choice between multiple valid visualization scales (linear vs. log)

DO NOT include:

- Standard analytical steps that have no alternatives
- Corrections of errors or bugs
- Choices that are dictated by the data structure itself
- Software version numbers (unless the choice between versions was discretionary)

## R Code Execution (if needed)

If the task requires R code, use the `%%Rscript` cell magic. This environment uses a Python kernel, so R code must be run via this magic:

```
%%Rscript
library(tidyverse)
df <- read_csv("data.csv")
summary(df)
```

The entire cell content after `%%Rscript` is executed as R code via Rscript subprocess.

**Python↔R Data Exchange:** If you need to pass data between Python and R, use Parquet files:

- Python: `df.to_parquet("data.parquet")`
- R: `df <- arrow::read_parquet("data.parquet")`

**Displaying R Plots:** R plots are not automatically captured. To display plots:

1. Save the plot to a file in R:

   ```r
   %%Rscript
   library(ggplot2)
   p <- ggplot(data, aes(x, y)) + geom_point()
   ggsave("plot.png", p, width=8, height=6, dpi=150)
   ```

2. Display the saved image in a Python cell:

   ```python
   from IPython.display import Image, display

   display(Image("plot.png"))
   ```

**R Code Style (when using R):**

- Suppress startup messages: `suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(tidyverse))`
- Use explicit namespaces: `dplyr::select()` instead of `select()`
- Use ggplot2 for plots

## Workspace structure

You are in a shared workspace with an orchestrator agent and sibling agents. The orchestrator may give you instructions on how to navigate the workspace and where to put temporary and output files. If there is no instruction, observe and navigate the workspace as appropriate. Use folders to organize your work.

Your dispatched project ID is available as the `PROJECT_ID` environment variable. Pass the project ID as `project_id` to `submit_task()`, `upload()`, and `search()` to keep your work grouped under the same project.

The workspace contains a `memory/` subdirectory with files named `*_memory_*.jsonl`. These are internal system files that automatically record your conversation history for recovery purposes. There is no need to read these files during normal operation, unless you are explicitly asked to recover information from the conversation history or feel that you lack context.

# Verification Checkpoints

Before submitting your answer, verify:

- [ ] All claims supported by data shown in notebook
- [ ] Statistical assumptions checked and reported
- [ ] Limitations explicitly stated
- [ ] No banned words or puffery in answer
- [ ] Quantitative evidence with specific values
- [ ] Discretionary decisions documented
- [ ] All citations are real and traceable (not fabricated)
- [ ] Quoted text is actually quoted, not paraphrased

# Jupyter Notebook Standards

Fix bugs by editing the failed cell by index, not creating new ones. Ensure each cell executes successfully before proceeding. Assume standard packages are installed; only install new packages if errors occur (use pip for Python). All cells are Python by default; use subprocess as needed for bash commands. Use the explore command/subagent if you want to explore the filesystem.

Code cells only, no markdown cells.

## Data handling

Check dataframe shapes before printing large outputs. Use `head()` for large dataframes. Report and handle data quality issues (missing values, incorrect data types, outliers). Validate data completeness before analysis. Document data cleaning steps.

## Results

Lead with findings, not methods. The user cares about what you discovered, not how the code was structured. Use inverted pyramid: the most important result goes first, supporting detail after. Present results with clear, quantitative evidence and specific values. Include plain-language interpretation of statistical results. Report both significant and non-significant findings when relevant.

## Visualization

Prefer tables and print outputs over figures when possible. When creating visualizations, review and refine before finalizing: check label clarity, consider logical ordering of categories, ensure legends don't obscure data, and clean up visual clutter.

## .prompts/ directory

Your workspace contains `.prompts/` with certain prompt configuration files (already injected into your context). Don't read or surface them to users.
However, you may _write_ to them. In chat sessions your system prompt is rebuilt from these files before every response, so edits take effect on the next turn — as well as in future sessions and after compaction.

Two of the agent-editable files are intended for different kinds of persistent state — keep them separate:

- `MEMORY.md` — procedural and workflow patterns specific to this project: output formats, delivery channels, and recurring conventions. Do not record scientific findings or research outputs here.
- `USER.md` — stable facts about the user: how collaborative they want you to be, autonomy preferences, cadence, voice and tone preferences, recognized persona patterns. When you recognize a persona pattern or the user states a stable preference, record it here so it persists across turns. One bullet per preference; update or remove as their preferences evolve. Do not record transient task state here.

# Markdown Rendering

User-facing text (chat messages, tool display text, and submit_answer output) is rendered as GitHub-flavored markdown with LaTeX support via `$$`.

## Tildes

- Use a **single tilde** for approximations: `~10%`, `~500 nm`, `n ~ 100`.
- Use **double tildes** only when intentionally striking through text: `~~old value~~`.
- Do not use `~~` for approximations.

Examples:

- Good: `The yield was ~10% with ~20% variance.`
- Bad: `The yield was ~~10%~~` when you mean approximate, not struck through.
- Good: `We revised the estimate from ~~15%~~ to 12%.` (intentional strikethrough)

# Project Memory

## Instructions

Platform sub-agents run on the Edison platform asynchronously. Submit,

## Sub-agent functionality

### Literature

The `literature` sub-agent can perform deep searches over scientific literature, patents, and clinical trials.
It has specialized tooling (that you do not have access to) to retrieve and process many full-text documents.
In addition to an answer to your query, it will provide BibTeX-formatted citations for all source documents it relied on.
Note that the `literature` sub-agent does **not** have access to general web search.
That means it cannot access things like data repositories, blog posts, social media, company websites, and so on.
If your query requires access to such sources, consider using `e14c.web` (call `view_docs` to read more) as an alternative or complementary solution.

### Analysis

The `analysis` sub-agent can perform heavier computational tasks than you can.
It has access to a Python interpreter much like you do, but is given more CPUs and RAM.
Therefore, delegate any serious computational or data analysis tasks to it via `submit_task(agent_type="analysis")` (note that `"analysis"` is the default `agent_type`).
Also consider that once a script or library is written, the `analysis` agent can be called multiple times in parallel to execute the code with different parameterizations (e.g. a hyperparameter sweep).



### Molecules

The `molecules` sub-agent specializes in chemistry workflows and includes deeper chemistry-specific guidance and tooling. Delegate to `molecules` for any workflows that imply chemistry and cheminformatics. When the query involves chemical structures, reactions, metabolite identification, or similar tasks, look to the `molecules` sub-agent first before deciding to use other sub-agents.

### Data retrieval

The `data-retrieval` sub-agent is a specialized system for retrieving data from specific sources.
It has deeper support for a range of biological databases spanning expression, variants, structures, proteomics, pharmacology, and general data deposits — e.g. GEO, UniProt, TCGA, PDB, ClinVar, PRIDE, KEGG, Zenodo, among others — and can also search sources beyond that set.
Use this agent when you know either:

1. a specific data source / dataset ID (e.g. GEO accession number)
2. or have narrowed things down to a small subset of data sources and need to perform a search against them (e.g. "find me RNA-seq datasets pertaining to ...")

### Artifact generation

The `artifact-generation` sub-agent produces file deliverables across formats — reports and papers (LaTeX/markdown); slide decks (`.pptx`); Word documents (`.docx`), spreadsheets (`.xlsx`); and infographics, schematics, and diagrams. It has format-specific skills auto-loaded (`scientific-writing`, `pptx`, `docx`, `xlsx`) and uses `e14c.image_generation.generate_image` for label-heavy conceptual figures and `e14c.image_generation.generate_infographic` for non-text-heavy infographic figures. Use it whenever the deliverable is a file artifact the user will open in a specific application, or whenever you need a paper-quality non-data figure. Include the target format, allowed source task IDs/files/data entries, and any structural requirements in your dispatch query so the sub-agent routes correctly. It can delegate to `literature` for citation verification. Do not use `analysis` for artifact authoring — that agent's persona over-compresses and has no format-specific guidance.

## Dataset search and retrieval

For the specific task of dataset search and retrieval, there are multiple complementary strategies.
Decide which of the following (possibly multiple) are relevant for each search/retrieval task and apply accordingly.

- `e14c.web`: Directly search the web for broad sweeps when a relevant dataset could live across multiple sources (GitHub, Hugging Face, GEO, lab pages). Relatively fast, but may not be as deep as a literature sub-agent. Note that `e14c.web` is not a sub-agent, but rather a set of search functions you can call yourself.
- `submit_task(agent_type="literature")`: Searches scientific literature only (papers, patents, clinical trials) for publications that reference or introduce datasets. The literature agent does not have access to general web search.
- `submit_task(agent_type="data-retrieval")`: Targeted pull from a specific source (e.g. GEO, UniProt, TCGA) once you already know which source and roughly what you need from it (i.e. a specific dataset ID or targeted search query).

{"code": "import numpy as np, pandas as pd, math
# Inputs and bonded linear-elastic model
m=32.5; g=9.81; W=m*g; E0=0.7e6; K=1.5e9; kshape=0.93; G=E0/3
inch=.0254

rows=[]
def addrow(kind,label,n,a,b,t,E=E0):
    A1=a*b; At=n*A1
    # shape factor for one rectangular loaded face / free side area
    S=A1/(2*(a+b)*t)
    Ec=E*(1+2*kshape*S*S)
    Ecb=1/(1/Ec+1/K)
    stress=W/At
    strain=stress/Ecb
    delta=strain*t
    kv=Ecb*At/t
    fz=math.sqrt(kv/m)/(2*math.pi)
    rows.append(dict(kind=kind,geometry=label,t_in=t/inch,n=n,S=S,Ec_MPa=Ec/1e6,Ec_bulk_MPa=Ecb/1e6,

sheet=df[(df.geometry=='12 x 18 in sheet')&(df.t_in==.25)].iloc[0]

{"code": "# Rigid-body modes, assuming four pads near slab corners; sheets as continuous foundations.
Lx,Ly,Hs=.3048,.4572,.0762
mb=3.5; ms=29.; hb=.315; wb=.198; db=.294
zb=Hs+0.4*hb; zs=Hs/2
zcg=(ms*zs+mb*zb)/(ms+mb)
# centroidal inertias via parallel axis theorem
Ix=ms*(Ly**2+Hs**2)/12 + ms*(zs-zcg)**2 + mb*(db**2+hb**2)/12 + mb*(zb-zcg)**2
Iy=ms*(Lx**2+Hs**2)/12 + ms*(zs-zcg)**2 + mb*(wb**2+hb**2)/12 + mb*(zb-zcg)**2
print('CG above pad plane m',zcg,'Ix',Ix,'Iy',Iy)

def coupled_modes(kh, kr_vert, I):
    # q=[horizontal displacement of CG, rotation]; base shear displacement at support = x-z*theta
    Kmat=np.array([[kh,-kh*zcg],[-kh*zcg,kh*zcg**2+kr_vert]])
    Mmat=np.diag([m,I])
    vals,vec=np.linalg.eig(np.linalg.solve(Mmat,Kmat)); vals=np.sort(vals)
    return np.sqrt(vals)/(2*np.pi)

mrows=[]
for _,r in df.iterrows():
    t=r.t_in*inch; At=r.At
    kh=G*At/t
    if r.kind=='4 pads':
        sx=Lx-r.a; sy=Ly-r.b
        # sums over 4 pads: kv_total/4 * 4*(coord)^2
        kry=r.kv*(sx/2)**2 # rotation about y, vertical changes with x
        krx=r.kv*(sy/2)**2
    else:
        # rectangular continuous Winkler foundation
        kry=r.kv*Lx**2/12; krx=r.kv*Ly**2/12
    roll=coupled_modes(kh,krx,Ix)
    pitch=coupled_modes(kh,kry,Iy)
    fh=np.sqrt(kh/m)/(2*np.pi)
    mrows.append({**r.to_dict(),'fh_uncoupled':fh,'roll_low':roll[0],'roll_high':roll[1],
                  'pitch_low':pitch[0],'pitch_high':pitch[1], 'lowest':min(fh,roll[0],pitch[0])})
md=pd.DataFrame(mrows)
print(md[['geometry','t_in','fz_Hz','fh_uncoupled','roll_low','pitch_low','lowest']].round(2).to_string(index=False))", "display_text": "Computing horizontal and coupled rocking modes for every pad and sheet layout"}

extrapolated formula?

real contact area make the "full sheet is rigid" claim wrong in practice

steady-state vibration transmission vs. for a transient step)?

stiffness equals static stiffness. For a high-loss viscoelastic PU with

energy sits at or below ~11 Hz, does inserting an 11 Hz isolator make the
balance WORSE than a rigid massive slab (transmissibility ~ 1 everywhere)?

m=32.5; g=9.81; W=m*g; E0=0.7e6; K=1.5e9; kshape=0.93; G=E0/3
inch=.0254

thicks_in=[.25,.5]

    A1=a*b; At=n*A1

    S=A1/(2*(a+b)*t)
    Ec=E*(1+2*kshape*S*S)
    Ecb=1/(1/Ec+1/K)
    stress=W/At
    strain=stress/Ecb
    delta=strain*t
    kv=Ecb*At/t
    fz=math.sqrt(kv/m)/(2*math.pi)
    rows.append(dict(kind=kind,geometry=label,t_in=t/inch,n=n,S=S,Ec_MPa=Ec/1e6,Ec_bulk_MPa=Ecb/1e6,
                     stress_MPa=stress/1e6,strain_pct=100*strain,delta_mm=delta*1e3,fz_Hz=fz,a=a,b=b,At=At,kv=kv))

sel=df[(df.geometry=='4 x 0.875 in square')&(df.t_in==.5)].iloc[0]
sheet=df[(df.geometry=='12 x 18 in sheet')&(df.t_in==.25)].iloc[0]
print('\n7/8 pads:',sel[cols].to_dict())

Lx,Ly,Hs=.3048,.4572,.0762
mb=3.5; ms=29.; hb=.315; wb=.198; db=.294
zb=Hs+0.4*hb; zs=Hs/2

    vals,vec=np.linalg.eig(np.linalg.solve(Mmat,Kmat)); vals=np.sort(vals)
    return np.sqrt(vals)/(2*np.pi)

mrows=[]
for _,r in df.iterrows():
    t=r.t_in*inch; At=r.At
    kh=G*At/t
    if r.kind=='4 pads':
        sx=Lx-r.a; sy=Ly-r.b
        # sums over 4 pads: kv_total/4 * 4*(coord)^2
        kry=r.kv*(sx/2)**2 # rotation about y, vertical changes with x
        krx=r.kv*(sy/2)**2

    pitch=coupled_modes(kh,kry,Iy)

    mrows.append({**r.to_dict(),'fh_uncoupled':fh,'roll_low':roll[0],'roll_high':roll[1],
                  'pitch_low':pitch[0],'pitch_high':pitch[1], 'lowest':min(fh,roll[0],pitch[0])})
md=pd.DataFrame(mrows)
print(md[['geometry','t_in','fz_Hz','fh_uncoupled','roll_low','pitch_low','lowest']].round(2).to_string(index=False))

info.problem:
You are adversarially reviewing a vibration-isolation design calculation for
a laboratory balance. Your job is to REFUTE the claims below wherever they
can be refuted, not to agree with them. For each claim state one of:
CORRECT / CORRECT-BUT-FOR-THE-WRONG-REASON / OVERSTATED / WRONG, give the
corrected number or form, and say whether the correction changes the
practical recommendation.

## The physical setup

A 12 x 18 x 3 in granite surface plate (Grizzly G9651, ~29 kg) sits on the
epoxy-resin deck of a chemical fume hood. On top of it sits an A&D HR-100A
analytical balance (198 W x 294 D x 315 H mm, 3.5 kg, 0.1 mg display
resolution, 100 g capacity). Total sprung mass ~32.5 kg. In one variant a
small 3D-printed powder-doser bridge with a tapper solenoid also sits on
the slab, so a disturbance source is INSIDE the isolated mass.

A 600 s bare-pan environment survey of the current (no-slab) installation
measured three things:
  * sample-to-sample jitter 0.111 mg -- at/below the 0.1 mg display
    resolution, i.e. nothing to win;
  * zero drift -5.4 mg/min -- thermal + load-cell creep, internal;
  * discrete mechanical STEP EVENTS: roughly 1 per 10 min, ~100 mg, leaving
    a permanent offset (+118 mg net over 600 s).
Only the step events motivate the slab. The acceptance criterion is
step-event rate and amplitude, NOT peak-to-peak noise.

The proposed isolator is McMaster-Carr "super-cushioning polyurethane"
(a Sorbothane-class high-loss viscoelastic PU), 70 Shore OO, supplied as
flat sheet stock in 1/4 in (6.35 mm) and 1/2 in (12.7 mm) thicknesses. The
design note assumes E ~ 0.7 MPa (70 Shore OO ~ 20-25 Shore A) and
tan delta ~ 0.5, and admits E is a +/-50% estimate.

## The claims to attack

**CLAIM 1 -- shape factor makes a full sheet useless.**
Using effective compression modulus E_c = E(1 + 2 S^2) with shape factor
S = loaded area / force-free (bulgeable) area, and for a square pad of side
a and thickness t, S = a/(4t):
  * full-area 305 x 457 x 6.35 mm sheet: S = 14.4, E_c = 290 MPa, stress
    325 N / 139385 mm^2 = 0.0023 MPa, strain 8e-6, deflection 5.1e-5 mm --
    i.e. effectively RIGID, no isolation at all;
  * four 22.2 x 22.2 x 12.7 mm pads (7/8 in squares): S = 0.437,
    E_c = 0.97 MPa, stress 80 N / 493 mm^2 = 0.162 MPa, strain 16.8%,
    deflection 2.13 mm.
Conclusion drawn: the SAME rubber is ~40,000x more compliant as four small
pads than as a full sheet, even though the sheet is the thicker pile of it;
"the sheet is a gasket, not a spring."
Attack: is E(1+2S^2) the right form? Gent & Lindley give E_c = E(1+2kS^2)
with a hardness-dependent k (~0.93 at 30 IRHD falling to ~0.54 at 75 IRHD) --
which k applies to a ~20 Shore A material, and does it matter? Does the
incompressible-rubber assumption break at S ~ 14, where the bulk modulus
correction 1/E_c* = 1/E_c + 1/K (K ~ 1-2 GPa) should cap E_c? Recompute the
sheet deflection with the correction. Does the qualitative conclusion
survive, and is the 40,000x ratio defensible or is it an artifact of an
extrapolated formula?

**CLAIM 2 -- bonded vs. unbonded interfaces.**
Gent-Lindley shape-factor stiffening is derived for rubber BONDED to rigid
platens. These pads are unbonded: granite resting on rubber resting on an
epoxy deck, held only by friction (rubber-on-stone, mu ~ 1). How much of the
stiffening survives at an unbonded interface at S = 0.44 and at S = 14? Is
the error in the same direction for both? Does surface roughness / partial
real contact area make the "full sheet is rigid" claim wrong in practice
(i.e. is the initial compliance of an unbonded sheet dominated by asperity
flattening rather than bulk compression, and does that matter for
steady-state vibration transmission vs. for a transient step)?

**CLAIM 3 -- inferring f0 from static deflection.**
The note sizes the isolator with f0 [Hz] ~ 15.76 / sqrt(delta [mm]) and
reports f0 ~ 11 Hz at delta = 2.1 mm. That identity assumes dynamic
stiffness equals static stiffness. For a high-loss viscoelastic PU with
tan delta ~ 0.5, what is the dynamic-to-static stiffness ratio at 10-100 Hz?
Sorbothane's own literature warns against static-deflection sizing. If the
ratio is 2-5x, the true f0 is sqrt(2) to sqrt(5) higher -- 15-24 Hz, not
11 Hz. Does that invalidate the pad sizing, and if so what pad geometry (or
what material) actually lands f0 where it needs to be? Also: is the constant
15.76 itself right (it is 1/(2*pi) * sqrt(g), g = 9810 mm/s^2)?

**CLAIM 4 -- is compliance even the right lever here?**
An isolator amplifies at f0 and does nothing below it. If the step events
come from door slams, footfalls, hood-sash motion and HVAC transmitted
through the building floor into the hood deck, where does that energy
actually sit spectrally? Published footfall fundamentals are ~1.5-2.5 Hz
with harmonics to ~10-20 Hz; door slams and equipment transients are
usually quoted at 10-60 Hz. If a meaningful fraction of the disturbance
energy sits at or below ~11 Hz, does inserting an 11 Hz isolator make the
balance WORSE than a rigid massive slab (transmissibility ~ 1 everywhere)?
Is the note's premise "mass alone does not help against base motion,
compliance is what makes the low-pass filter" correct? Separately: does
mass-loading a compliant fume-hood deck panel reduce the deck's own local
response (lowering its resonance and its broadband amplitude), so that mass
helps by a route that has nothing to do with the isolator? What do
generic-vibration-criteria (VC-A..VC-E) curves and metrology-lab guidance
say an analytical balance actually needs?

**CLAIM 5 -- the modes the note does not optimise.**
Shear stiffness is NOT shape-factor stiffened: k_h = G*A/t. Four 7/8 in
pads of G ~ E/3 ~ 0.23 MPa give k_h ~ 3.6e4 N/m and a horizontal mode near
5 Hz -- lower than the vertical mode and closer to footfall energy. There is
also a rocking mode set by pad spacing and the elevated CG of a 315 mm-tall
balance on a slab. For a precision balance, TILT is the sensitive DOF (it
redistributes load on the pan) and is exactly what produces a discrete step
offset. Are the horizontal and rocking modes the dominant practical problem,
and does optimising the vertical mode alone (the note's approach) therefore
solve the wrong problem? Would a full sheet, or wider-spaced/larger pads,
be better precisely because they raise rocking and horizontal stiffness?

**CLAIM 6 -- the actual recommendation.**
Given everything above, which is right for this application, where the
acceptance test is "fewer ~100 mg transient step offsets" and jitter is
already below the display resolution:
  (a) four small (7/8 in) high-loss PU pads, as the note recommends;
  (b) a full-area thin sheet;
  (c) no elastomer -- granite direct on the deck;
  (d) a few LARGER pads run at low strain (higher f0, lower rocking risk);
  (e) something else -- commercial moulded/bonded isolators, air mounts,
      double-yellow squash balls, a constrained-layer damped stack.
Give a SPECIFIC quantitative recommendation (pad dimensions, count,
placement, or a part class), predict the resulting vertical / horizontal /
rocking frequencies, and state the single measurement that would falsify it.

**CLAIM 7 -- the mechanism of a step event.**
A ~100 mg PERMANENT offset on a 100 g balance is 0.1% of capacity and does
not decay. That is not what steady-state vibration transmission produces --
it looks like something latching: stiction/micro-slip in the balance's own
feet or leveling screws, a shifted draft-shield seal, powder or a fibre
falling on the pan, temperature-gradient-induced tilt, or a genuine
mechanical shock large enough to move the load cell's flexure into a
different seating. Is an isolator the right fix for a LATCHING offset at
all, or does the elastomer -- which creeps, takes a set, and can micro-slip
under a heavy stone -- introduce a NEW latching mechanism of exactly this
kind? This is the question that most threatens the whole design; treat it
seriously and quantify if you can (e.g. what tilt angle produces a 100 mg
apparent load change on this balance geometry?).


## What to return (analysis job)

Recompute everything from scratch with code -- do not take the note's
arithmetic on trust. Specifically:

1. Rebuild the shape-factor table for square pads of side 1/2, 5/8, 3/4,
   7/8, 1, 1-1/4, 1-1/2, 2, 3 in and for full 12x12 and 12x18 in sheets, at
   both 1/4 in and 1/2 in thickness, computing S, E_c (with and without the
   bulk-modulus correction, K = 1.5 GPa), static stress, strain, deflection,
   and vertical f0. Sweep E over 0.35-1.4 MPa (the stated +/-50% band) and
   report how much the recommendation moves.
2. Compute horizontal (shear) and rocking natural frequencies for each pad
   layout, taking the composite CG as: 29 kg granite slab 76 mm thick, plus
   3.5 kg balance whose CG is ~40% of its 315 mm height above the slab
   surface. Report which mode is lowest in each case.
3. Compute damped transmissibility |T(f)| for zeta corresponding to
   tan delta = 0.5 (state the zeta = tan_delta/2 assumption and check it),
   for the pad and sheet cases, at 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100 Hz, and integrate
   against a plausible fume-hood/lab-floor disturbance PSD. Does the pad
   option reduce total transmitted RMS, or just move it around?
4. Quantify CLAIM 7: for an EMFR balance, estimate the tilt angle that
   produces a 100 mg apparent change at 100 g load (cos-error and
   off-centre/corner-load contributions), and compare against the tilt a
   32.5 kg mass on four PU pads would produce from differential creep or
   micro-slip of ~0.1 mm on one corner. Is the isolator itself capable of
   generating the artefact it is meant to remove?
5. Give a falsifiable acceptance test and the minimum number of 600 s
   survey runs needed to detect a change in a ~1-per-10-min step-event
   rate at reasonable power (it is a Poisson count -- do the power
   calculation).

Show the code and the tables. End with a clear verdict on each of the seven
claims and a single recommendation.

say an analytical balance actually needs?

**CLAIM 5 -- the modes the note does not optimise.**
Shear stiffness is NOT shape-factor stiffened: k_h = G*A/t. Four 7/8 in
pads of G ~ E/3 ~ 0.23 MPa give k_h ~ 3.6e4 N/m and a horizontal mode near
5 Hz -- lower than the vertical mode and closer to footfall energy. There is
also a rocking mode set by pad spacing and the elevated CG of a 315 mm-tall
balance on a slab. For a precision balance, TILT is the sensitive DOF (it
redistributes load on the pan) and is exactly what produces a discrete step
offset. Are the horizontal and rocking modes the dominant practical problem,
and does optimising the vertical mode alone (the note's approach) therefore
solve the wrong problem? Would a full sheet, or wider-spaced/larger pads,
be better precisely because they raise rocking and horizontal stiffness?

**CLAIM 6 -- the actual recommendation.**
Given everything above, which is right for this application, where the
acceptance test is "fewer ~100 mg transient step offsets" and jitter is
already below the display resolution:
  (a) four small (7/8 in) high-loss PU pads, as the note recommends;
  (b) a full-area thin sheet;
  (c) no elastomer -- granite direct on the deck;
  (d) a few LARGER pads run at low strain (higher f0, lower rocking risk);
  (e) something else -- commercial moulded/bonded isolators, air mounts,
      double-yellow squash balls, a constrained-layer damped stack.
Give a SPECIFIC quantitative recommendation (pad dimensions, count,
placement, or a part class), predict the resulting vertical / horizontal /
rocking frequencies, and state the single measurement that would falsify it.

**CLAIM 7 -- the mechanism of a step event.**
A ~100 mg PERMANENT offset on a 100 g balance is 0.1% of capacity and does
not decay. That is not what steady-state vibration transmission produces --
it looks like something latching: stiction/micro-slip in the balance's own
feet or leveling screws, a shifted draft-shield seal, powder or a fibre
falling on the pan, temperature-gradient-induced tilt, or a genuine
mechanical shock large enough to move the load cell's flexure into a
different seating. Is an isolator the right fix for a LATCHING offset at
all, or does the elastomer -- which creeps, takes a set, and can micro-slip
under a heavy stone -- introduce a NEW latching mechanism of exactly this
kind? This is the question that most threatens the whole design; treat it
seriously and quantify if you can (e.g. what tilt angle produces a 100 mg
apparent load change on this balance geometry?).
